new_statements.reading: Burmese has no word-stress system independent of tone. Prominence belongs to tone-bearing major (heavy) syllables, each of which is its own foot; toneless schwa minor syllables are unfooted and never word-final, so a word's final syllable is always a tone-bearing major syllable. Because (L L) feet do not exist, the foot's headedness (trochaic vs iambic) cannot be determined from stress placement (Green 2005 later calls it left-headed on mora-internal grounds). This agrees with Watkins 2001 p. 293 ('Stress is subordinate to tone in Burmese') and with the catalog's 'tonal' coding; it refines it by giving the foot/word-shape account of which syllables are prominent (major, tone-bearing) and which are reduced (schwa minor syllables).

sources.quote: there is good reason to suppose that the foot in Burmese is not an iamb—either (L 'H) or ('H)—but rather a single heavy syllable ('H) only. In this case, light syllables in [L H], [L L H], and [H L H] words would remain unfooted [p. 11] ... (In Burmese and Thai—discussed below—tone-bearing syllables fill the role of stressed syllables.) As mentioned in the discussion of major and minor syllables above, Burmese allows words of the shape [L «H] and [«H], but not [L «L]. [p. 13]
sources.note: First-hand theoretical analysis: Burmese has no stress system separate from tone; the tone-bearing major (heavy) syllable is the foot and plays the role of the stressed syllable, while minor schwa syllables are unfooted (NON-FOOT(schwa)) and every word must end in a major syllable (ALIGN-R). Whether the (H) foot is trochaic or iambic is undecidable because (L L) feet do not exist (p. 13). Polysyllabic words of several major syllables are several feet/prosodic words, i.e. no single culminative word stress is posited.

sources.quote: Tones are syllabic, in central Burmese as well as in other Burmese dialects … It is generally admitted that there are four tonemes: creaky, low, breathy, and glottal stop; three of them occur on open syllables and on syllables with either a nasalized vowel nucleus, or a nasalizing effect on the initial of the following syllable; the fourth toneme implies the existence of an unreleased glottal stop at the end of the syllable. … But if we consider it as a contrastive element belonging to the phonemic structure of the syllable and not to its tonemic structure, there would be three tonemes only.

tone.quote: Just such a trace element exists in the so-called ‘creaky tone' of Burmese: ?auk mrac! … The tone and its statistical distribution. Within Modern Burmese, three tones are found in non-stopped syllables: the level tone, the "heavy' tone [hre?pauk], and the creaky tone [?auk mrac]. The creaky tone is by far the least frequently occurring Burmese tone (only about 350 words are found under ?auk mrac) but it is now scattered through the Modern Burmese lexicon. It is found as the lexical tone of at least some members of every word class

tone.quote: Tone-Pattern I. Burmese Tone 3 (Level Rising) usually corresponds to Tone 4 in P'u-t'ao Lisu … Tone-Pattern II. Burmese Tone 4 (Released Falling), while generally corresponding to Tone 5 in Lisu, may cover all three Even Tones in both dialects … Tone-Pattern III. Burmese Tone 2 (Short Falling). This tone is often indicated in Old Burmese script, but the words, though common, are few compared to those in the two other tones. … Stops. These, in Burmese, are not tonally significant; and since they end abruptly are, ipso facto, difficult to fit into a tonal system.
